en: *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, one fascicle; excerpted from the *Nirākāra-vāda-śāstra*, translated by Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
All three realms consist solely of consciousness (*vijñapti*). What, then, constitutes these? There are two kinds of the three realms.
Consciousness:
first, manifesting consciousness; second, discriminating consciousness.
Manifesting consciousness is the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna); this fundamental consciousness transforms into the five sense objects, the four great elements, and so forth.
What is the discriminating consciousness?

It is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which, within manifest consciousness, discriminates and constructs [concepts of] humans and devas, long and short, large and small, male and female, trees, vines, and all such things—discriminating all phenomena.
This collection of consciousnesses that discriminates mental objects (*dharmas*) is called the discriminating consciousness.
Just as the appearance of reflected forms arises in dependence upon a mirror, so too does the discriminating consciousness arise in dependence upon the manifesting consciousness.

When this discrimination arises, it establishes the power of perfuming within the ālayavijñāna; by virtue of this power of perfuming, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is able to arise in the future, and conditioned by this future manifesting consciousness (nirbhāsavijñāna), the future discriminating consciousness is able to arise.
Based on this causal principle, there is therefore no sequence of before or after in birth and death.
To clarify this meaning, the Buddha spoke a verse in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Sūtra on the Analysis of the Sections):
"Manifest consciousness gives rise to discrimination; Discrimination gives rise to perfuming."
"Through perfuming, manifesting consciousness arises; thus the wheel of birth and death revolves.
As for what is called "perfuming," there are two: first, the habitual attachment to the nature of false discrimination; second, the cultivation of the contemplation of the true nature.
Based on these two meanings, it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).
Regarding the first perfuming, it increases the *ālayavijñāna*.

Once the *ālayavijñāna* has been increased, it becomes fully endowed with all capacities; it can produce the six destinies and the various consciousnesses that undergo rebirth. For this reason, birth and death are brought to completion.
The second type of perfuming is called the cultivation of the true nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); this perfuming is able to eliminate attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Because the first type of perfuming has been impaired, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is also impaired.
Once the *ālayavijñāna* is impaired, the consciousness that undergoes rebirth is also impaired.
Since the *ālayavijñāna* is capable of generating the three realms, by virtue of its impairment, the transformation of the three realms is attained.
Based on this meaning of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), there are five aspects, as explained in the section on the characteristics of the distinctions of cessation.
Manifesting consciousnesses (*vijñapti*) are of nine kinds:

first, body-consciousness; second, object-consciousness; third, activity-consciousness; fourth, time-consciousness; fifth, vessel-consciousness; sixth, number-consciousness; seventh, fourfold linguistic consciousness; eighth, consciousness of the distinction between self and others; and ninth, consciousness of good, evil, and birth-and-death.
Next, the discernment of consciousness is of two kinds:
first, the consciousness of the possessor of a body; second, the consciousness of the experiencer.

Among the preceding nine consciousnesses, the first is the consciousness of the body, which means it transforms into that which resembles a body; therefore, this consciousness is named "body-consciousness."
Regarding the term "resembling" (*sādṛśya*): just as the perceived characteristics of the body resemble a body but are not the actual reality, it is called a "resembling body.
This consciousness can produce something resembling a body and is thus termed "body-consciousness" (*kāyavijñāna*), which refers to the five sense faculties.
The other eight types of consciousness, such as those of form and so forth, are likewise thus; this is precisely the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

As for what is called "body-consciousness" (*kāya-vijñāna*), there are five kinds, namely the sense-sphere of the eye-faculty and so forth; these are termed body-consciousness because they pertain to all five faculties.

The second, the consciousness of objects (*viṣayavijñāna*), has six types: from the sphere of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānaviṣaya*); these are collectively termed the consciousness of what is to be experienced (*vedanīyavijñāna*).
The third, the consciousness of function (*karmavijñāna*), consists of the six types of the visual-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) and so forth; that is, the six consciousnesses.
The *Mahā-śāstra* refers to this as "consciousness of correct reception.
Regarding the fourth, "consciousness of the three times," there are three types, namely the three periods of time: past, future, and present.
Furthermore, it is called "world" (*loka*) because the continuity of birth and death is uninterrupted.
Regarding the fifth, the "receptacle-consciousness" (*bhājana-vijñāna*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it the "locus-consciousness.

Briefly stated, this refers to the receptacle world, meaning the external four great elements and five sense objects; extensively stated, it refers to the ten directions, the three realms, and so forth.
The sixth, the reckoning-consciousness, consists of calculation and measurement.
The seventh, the fourfold verbalizing-consciousness, refers to the four types: seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.
All verbal expressions do not transcend these four; if one does not speak of what is seen, one speaks of what is heard, and the same applies to what is sensed and cognized.
Regarding the eighth [category], the distinct consciousnesses of self and others, this refers to the fact that their bases are different and their six destinies are not the same.
The "basis" refers to the body; the bodies of the six destinies refer to the distinct consciousnesses of oneself and others.

Regarding the ninth consciousness, which pertains to birth and death within the good and evil destinies: all birth and death does not transcend these two paths—the good being the realms of humans and devas, and the evil being the four miserable destinies.
These paths of good and evil do not transcend birth and death, for they arise and perish in the very moment without remaining.
Furthermore, those who possess a body and consciousness are shrouded by the view of self.
Because this consciousness is shrouded by the view of self and craving, it undergoes birth within the six destinies.

This consciousness constitutes the body of birth and death; if this consciousness exists, then there is the body-consciousness, and if this consciousness is exhausted, then the body of birth and death is exhausted.
Because the view of self gives rise to all delusions regarding flesh, and craving gives rise to all delusions regarding skin, there exists the body of birth and death.
If one is free from craving and the view of self, then the afflictions of skin and flesh will cease to exist.
If there were no afflictions of skin and flesh, there would be no body within the three realms; therefore, it is the body-consciousness that undergoes birth and death.
Second is the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādāna-vijñāna*); the mental realm (*manodhātu*) is called the appropriating consciousness, which consists of three types of mental consciousness:

first, the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which is the subtle-grade mental consciousness that constantly receives karmic retribution, is not associated with good or evil, and is exclusively non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Second is the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness), which is the medium-grade mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that receives only the karmic retribution of an ordinary person’s body;

third is what is called the constantly manifest mental consciousness, which is the coarse-grade mental consciousness that universally receives the fruits of the three natures: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
The five consciousnesses are likewise so.
These three categories of mental consciousness are all capable of experiencing karmic retribution;
however, as the present discussion concerns their arising and ceasing, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is specifically termed the "experiencing consciousness."

Furthermore, the ālayavijñāna is the locus of the "self" as conceived by ordinary beings; because the *ādānavijñāna* grasps the ālayavijñāna as its object of the self, and it is precisely this *ādānavijñāna* that constitutes the grasper.
Because the seven consciousnesses constitute the essence of the view of self, there are two kinds of discerning consciousness:
first, the consciousness of the body (kāya-vijñāna), and second, the consciousness of the possessor of the body (dehin-vijñāna); these together are termed the mental faculty (manas-indriya).

The root of defilement in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* is the *ādāna-vijñāna*. The second, the sequential dependent mental faculty (*manas*), takes the fundamental consciousness as its object and conceives it as a self; from this, the appearances of that object emerge, manifesting nine kinds of consciousness.
As explained above, consciousness is exclusively the ālayavijñāna; if it is the discriminating consciousness, it consists of the *manas* and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The *manas* discriminates the self, while the mental consciousness discriminates the myriad dharmas.

The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses three types of discrimination (*vikalpa*), whereas the five sensory consciousnesses possess only discrimination by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavikalpa*).
There are four kinds of skillful means for the perfuming (*vāsanā*):
first, patience (*kṣānti*); second, names (*nāman*); third, characteristics (*nimitta*); and fourth, the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
There are two types of patience:
first, the extensive; second, the concise.

All sentient beings are deluded regarding true nature; now, in their practice, they first perform the extensive contemplation and subsequently perform the concise contemplation, thereby attaining entry into reality.

What is called "extensive" refers to the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its accumulation (*samudaya*) constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of ordinary beings; cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) constitute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Each of these has nine aspects. Regarding the ninefold contemplation of suffering: within the three realms (*tridhātu*), each possesses the three periods of time (*tryadhvan*), thus forming nine.
Furthermore, there is one *bhava* (existence) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), four in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and four in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), thus making nine types.

The nine divisions of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*) are precisely the nine divisions of the fetters (*saṃyojana*); the cessation of these nine fetters constitutes the nine truths of cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Regarding the nine divisions of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), these are the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), which are the nine successive meditative absorptions (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

Next, regarding the brief contemplation in which the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) is first contemplated as being of eight kinds: one contemplates the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four names (*nāma*). The four great elements constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and the four names constitute the four [mental] aggregates (*skandha*); thus, they are taken as the eight kinds.
Regarding the eight types of the truth of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*): these are the eight wrong paths (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*) that deviate from the eightfold noble path.
Regarding the eight kinds of the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*): the cessation of the eight wrong paths is itself termed the eight kinds of cessation.
Regarding the eight [factors] of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*): cultivating the eightfold noble path constitutes the truth of the path.
Next, one further briefly contemplates suffering as sevenfold: the six realms of existence (*ṣadgati*) and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the sevenfold accumulation (*samudaya*), these are the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The seven underlying tendencies are greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, and views. Within these, the desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is called the underlying tendency of desire (*kāma-anuśaya*); that which pertains to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) is called the underlying tendency of existence (*bhava-anuśaya*). Combined, these constitute the seven kinds of underlying tendencies. The cessation of these seven underlying tendencies is termed the sevenfold cessation.
The seven factors of the Truth of the Path are the seven limbs of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
Next, one briefly contemplates suffering as being of six kinds, namely the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmikāyatana*).
The six kinds of origination refer to the six kinds of craving; that is, the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) give rise to the six kinds of craving.
The extinction of the six types of craving constitutes the six extinctions. Regarding the sixfold path, there are six kinds of realms of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*):

first, the realm of cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to renounce hatred that harms others; second, the realm of cultivating compassion (*karuṇā*) to renounce hatred that oppresses and afflicts; third, the realm of cultivating sympathetic joy (*muditā*) to renounce hatred that is jealous; fourth, the realm of cultivating equanimity (*upekṣā*) to renounce sensual desire; fifth, the realm of cultivating mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation to renounce the influence of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); and sixth, the realm of cultivating non-self (*anātman*) to renounce the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Cultivating these six kinds is called the realm of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*).
Next, one briefly contemplates suffering as fivefold, namely the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
and origination as fivefold, namely the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*).
The extinction of these five hindrances constitutes the five kinds of extinction.
As for the fivefold path, it consists of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five powers (*pañcabala*), among others.
Next, one briefly contemplates the four aspects of suffering, which are the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*): namely, body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
Regarding the "four aggregates," these are the four graspings (*upādāna*) and are also the four floods (*ogha*).

As for the four graspings, "grasping" is simply craving; there are four kinds of craving, which constitute the four types of grasping: first, the grasping of sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*); second, the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*);
third, the grasping of precepts and vows (*śīlavratopādāna*); and fourth, the grasping of the theory of self (*ātmavādopādāna*).

The grasping of self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*) refers to internal grasping conditioned by the internal five aggregates; it is the craving for the internal dharmas of the eight dhyānas of the form and formless realms, which is called the grasping of self-theory.
Within this, "grasping" is termed the grasping of self-theory.
If one craves the objects of the desire realm, they are called external phenomena and are termed "clinging to desire" (*kāma-upādāna*).

Those who cling to desire are beings with the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), while clinging to the discourse of self (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*) refers to beings with the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); based on these two factors, they give rise to clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and clinging to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).
The grasping of the view of permanence arises conditioned by principle.
These four graspings are the provisions for feeling (*vedanā*).
It should be understood that there are three kinds of craving for feeling (*vedanā-tṛṣṇā*):
First, craving for detachment refers to all sentient beings in the three miserable realms.
Second, craving for seeking attainment refers to those from humans and devas up to the three formless attainments.
Third, craving for abiding refers to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which is regarded as *nirvāṇa*.
The four kinds of grasping are called the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The cessation of the four kinds of grasping is called the four truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
As for the four aspects of the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), they refer to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which are themselves the four kinds of wisdom (*prajñā*).

Contemplating the body leads to the thorough penetration of the Truth of Suffering; contemplating sensation leads to the thorough penetration of the Truth of Origination; contemplating the mind leads to the thorough penetration of the Truth of Cessation; and contemplating phenomena leads to the thorough penetration of the Truth of the Path.

One contemplates the body as coarse; one contemplates the coarseness of the bodies within the three realms as suffering; one contemplates the cold, heat, and so forth of the bodies in the desire realm as suffering; one contemplates the four modes of deportment of the bodies in the form realm as suffering; and one contemplates the moment-to-moment instability of the minds in the formless realm as suffering.

Regarding the observation of feeling (vedanā) to penetrate the truth of origination (samudaya-satya): because all craving and attachment of sentient beings arise conditioned by feeling, and since craving does not arise in the absence of feeling, one observes feeling to penetrate the truth of origination.

If one contemplates the mind and penetrates the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one sees that all sentient beings establish the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within their minds; therefore, because sentient beings cling to this view of self, they do not believe in cessation. This is solely because the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) clings to the *ādānavijñāna* as being unitary and eternal, and thus the essence of the self is not subject to cessation.
By contemplating that the mind is not the self, one believes in cessation in order to abandon the view of self.
By contemplating the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—one contemplates the mind and penetrates the truth of cessation.
Regarding the contemplation of phenomena that penetrates the truth of the path, there are two types of phenomena:
There are two categories: the impure category and the pure category.
One contemplates the impure category as suffering and its origin, and regards pure phenomena as cessation and the path.
Furthermore, since the impure category consists of all afflictions and the pure category consists of all remedial paths, one must thoroughly penetrate the Truth of the Path.
Next, one briefly contemplates the three types of suffering, which is to contemplate the three realms as suffering:
one contemplates the desire realm as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

one contemplates the form realm as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), because birth and abiding do not cease, and when pleasure changes, it is immediately suffering; thus it is the suffering of change.
One contemplates the formless realm as the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), for its arising, abiding, and destruction are all suffering.
Sentient beings, however, have two paths: the evil realms are suffering and the wholesome realms are happiness; abandoning these two extremes is called Nirvana.
This mind involves activity and movement; therefore, because it is impermanent, it is suffering.
There are three types of accumulation, namely the three poisons, as well as three other kinds:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Regarding the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): sentient beings are attached to this view, clinging to the notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; consequently, they dwell in birth and death and do not cultivate the supramundane path.
Regarding the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): they are unwilling to practice the true path.
"Doubt" refers to uncertainty and lack of decisive understanding.
The Truth of Cessation extinguishes these three kinds of afflictions, which constitutes the three types of cessation.
As for the "threefold Path," it refers to ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Next, briefly observing suffering as twofold refers to body and mind;
it is also called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As for the two aspects of origination, within the twelve links of dependent origination they refer to ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The cessation of these two types constitutes the two kinds of cessation.
The two aspects of the Truth of the Path are concentration and wisdom.
Next, one briefly contemplates suffering as a single category, namely that impermanence is suffering.
"Accumulation" refers to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
The cessation of this mental attention constitutes "cessation.

The "path" refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), which is the collective contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness termed the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, according to another interpretation, correct reflection constitutes the Truth of the Path, while incorrect reflection constitutes the Truth of Origination; this is for the purpose of making true wisdom distinct and clear.
One contemplates suffering through both extensive and concise modes of observation, analyzing all phenomena into nine parts down to a single part; the same applies to the remaining three Truths.
There are four types of bases for the habitual tendencies of language and discrimination. Regarding the habitual tendencies of language:
they range from the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "names" (*nāman*) up to the stage of the "dharmas of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-dharma*).
What is called "locus" (sthāna) refers to that which is reached, namely the objective sphere as the locus.
Through the differentiation of habitual perfuming, one proceeds from the [phenomenal] marks up to the first of all dharmas attained through cultivation.
Regarding all those who have attained the state of cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha-dharmasthāna*), from the inferior grade up to the superior grade, all such stages constitute the locus (*sthāna*).
If a person relies on names (*nāman*) for analytical discernment (*pravicaya*), this is called the perfuming of language (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*);
if a person, apart from names, phrases (*pada*), and so forth, directly discerns the meaning (*artha*), this is called the perfuming of discrimination (*vikalpa-vāsanā*).
This clarifies the latter two types of consciousness.
These two types of consciousness are:
first, the consciousness of fourfold discourse; second, the consciousness of the distinction between self and other. This clarifies these two types of consciousness.
The other seven types of consciousness and the discriminating consciousness—these eight types of consciousness arise by taking the perfuming of language as their object.
Furthermore, there are two types of consciousness:
first, the body-consciousness; second, the recipient-consciousness.

Furthermore, the three consciousnesses—the self-consciousness, the other-consciousness, and the distinct-consciousness—arise by taking the perfuming of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as their object-condition.
Moreover, the consciousnesses of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and birth-and-death arise by taking the perfuming of the *bhavāṅga* (constituent of existence) as their object-condition.

These various consciousnesses are what is meant by the principle that "all three realms consist of nothing but consciousness. Regarding the ninth section on the nine consciousnesses, there are two parts to the combined explanation of the text and its meaning:
first, clarifying the essence of consciousness; second, clarifying the function of consciousness.
Regarding the "single essence of consciousness," it appears in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
The treatise states:
"All that exists within the three realms is nothing but consciousness."
Question:
All phenomena (*dharma*) are simply the three realms (*tridhātu*); what is the use of two terms?
Answer:
There are two meanings.

First, "all" refers to the four types of birth and death: the *paricchinna* (segmented) within the three realms and the *pariṇāma* (transformative) beyond the realms; second, it refers to "all" in its broadest sense.
What are the ten directions? The ten directions are not the three realms; therefore, it is said that "all" refers to the three realms.

Now, regarding "there is only consciousness": the aforementioned seven kinds of death are manifested by consciousness alone; apart from consciousness, they have no separate substance. Therefore, it is said that the three realms consist of nothing but consciousness.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*).
There are two aspects to intrinsic nature:
first, the sense of non-intermixture; for instance, the nature of desire is distinct from form, and form is not the same as the formless.

Second, "nature" (svabhāva) has the meaning of being unchanging and non-transforming: desire remains desire, form remains form, and the formless remains the formless; likewise with the wholesome and the unwholesome—the three natures do not change, which is the meaning.
"Consciousness-only" means that apart from consciousness, there are no separate objects.
It is through consciousness that objects appear as if they exist; apart from consciousness, objects have no intrinsic nature.
The treatise says:
What constitutes consciousness?
It refers to the three realms.
The commentary states:
The previous section clarified that the three realms do not exist apart from consciousness; this section clarifies that consciousness does not exist apart from the three realms.
Furthermore, the previous section elucidated the functions of the two types of consciousness.
The treatise states:
Consciousness is of two kinds: first, manifest consciousness; second, discriminating consciousness.
The commentary states:
the former is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); this fundamental consciousness manifests the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
The next one refers to the six consciousnesses; these six consciousnesses differentiate "this" from "that.
Furthermore, the former clarifies the object-condition (*ālambana*), while the latter clarifies the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*).
Regarding the manifest consciousness, there are two types of transformation (*pariṇāma*):
The first transformation produces the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); the second transformation produces the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Next, the evolving consciousness transforms into that which resembles a self.

Thus, the manas clings to these two consciousnesses as being the self; that is, the *ālayavijñāna* (here referred to as *dhana*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) together produce the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), grasping its own essence, gives rise to the appearance of a self-body; this is because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates and calculates that the self possesses various distinct functions.
All phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent: because the six objects exist, there are the six consciousnesses, so they cannot be definitively non-existent;
yet, apart from the six consciousnesses, there are no six objects, so they cannot be definitively existent.

Furthermore, all phenomena cannot be definitively said to exist, nor can they be definitively said not to exist; because the two selves—the self of persons and the self of phenomena—are unreal, they cannot be said to exist, yet because the emptiness of these two is ultimate reality, they cannot be said not to exist.

Furthermore, there is another meaning: all phenomena are definitively existent and definitively non-existent. While persons and phenomena are definitively non-existent, this twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena is definitively existent.
These three together reveal that the conventional is existent and the ultimate is non-existent.
Second, the explanation of the functioning of consciousness.
The treatise states:
When this discriminating consciousness arises, it establishes the power of perfuming within the ālayavijñāna.
The commentary states:

Regarding the power of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is like when incense is burned to perfume a garment; although the substance of the incense has perished, its fragrance remains within the garment, and this is called "perfumed clothing."
This fragrance cannot be said to exist, because the substance of the fragrance has perished;
nor can it be said not to exist, because the scent remains. Therefore, it is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).

Just as the six consciousnesses give rise to good and evil, which leave behind the power of perfuming within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), enabling the attainment of future retribution; this is termed a "seed" (*bīja*).
If according to the tenets of the Hīnayāna, the Saṃmitīya school’s position is called "without fault," being like a promissory note.
Thus the Buddha spoke this verse:
"Karmas are not lost; Throughout incalculable eons, Until the time of their accumulation..."
"It is for the sake of rewarding sentient beings.
The Mahāsāṃghika school calls this "the grasping of consciousness" (*saṃgraha-vijñāna*), which is a factor dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

It is like reciting a scripture: on the first repetition, one has not yet mastered it; on the second repetition, one grasps what was previously recited on the first; and so on, until at the tenth repetition, when one has attained fluency, one simultaneously grasps all nine preceding repetitions.

In this way, the initial consciousness undergoes transformation within the first [stage], and so on until the ninth transformation occurs within the tenth; the tenth is able to encompass the preceding nine, and this functional capacity of the tenth transformation is termed "the consciousness of integration" (*saṃgraha-vijñāna*).
Because there are the functions of the preceding nine, the preceding nine are not lost.

In the Sarvāstivāda school, this is termed "simultaneous acquisition" (*samanvāgama*). "Simultaneous" (*sama*) refers to its correspondence with number, locus, time, and so forth; "conformity" (*anu*) refers to its non-obstruction with the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*); and "acquisition" (*lābha*) has the meaning of non-loss. Thus, both "simultaneous" and "conformity" signify non-loss.

For example, it is like the *mudu-lou*—this refers to the flower of the *yu* tree. One takes the juice of the *ruo-ke*—meaning a red-colored juice—and applies it to the filaments of the *mudu-lou* flower. The filaments become red along with the juice; later, when the fruit forms and ripens, the red color emerges. This is called "attainment through simultaneous cultivation."
Because the red color reaches the fruit without being lost, it is called "identical" (*sabhāga*).
Because the red color emerges prior to that identity, it is called "identical cultivation and attainment" (*sabhāga-bhāvanā-lābha*).

Because the red color reaches the fruit without being lost, it is called "identical"; because what came before reaches what follows without being lost, it is called "conforming" (*anuvartin*); and because it is manifested at the very end, it is called "attainment" (*lābha*).
If it is according to the Saṃmitīya school, it is called the "appropriating consciousness" (bhavāṅga-vijñāna).
"Existence" (bhava) refers to the three realms of existence;
there are also seven types of existence:

There are four types of existence (*bhava*): first, intermediate existence (*antarābhava*); second, birth existence (*upapattibhava*); third, karmic existence (*karmabhava*); and fourth, death existence (*maraṇabhava*). Together with the aforementioned three existences, these constitute the seven existences.
The two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*) possess all four existences; however, the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks intermediate existence.
"Existing therein" refers precisely to that which is called "tending toward the place of birth.
A "place" (sthāna) is so named because it possesses causes and conditions.
It is like the members of the twelve links of dependent origination: because this thing exists, that thing exists; because this thing arises, that thing arises.
"Existence" refers to the cause; there are two types of causes:
first, the antecedent cause; second, the simultaneous cause.
For example, when a mandarin orange produces a sprout, this is an antecedent cause; once the sprout has arisen, it exists simultaneously with the orange.

Simultaneous causes refer to the fact that volitional formations condition consciousness, consciousness conditions name-and-form, name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, and the six sense bases condition contact, feeling, and so forth—all of which occur simultaneously.
The reason it is said that "because this exists, that exists" is to refute the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of arising-existence (*jāti-bhava*).
The external doctrine states:
"All sentient beings arise from the self of Maheśvara; therefore, birth and death exist. The internal doctrine is said to be the same as this.
Now, [the internal position] refutes this by asserting that birth occurs because it arises from prior causes.
You, Īśvara, do not exist; you are not born, yet you are subject to birth and death. Because such birth exists, you cannot be said to exist.
Since you cannot be said to exist, therefore you do exist.

Therefore, the Buddha’s established doctrine is that the existence of a thing is precisely its arising; your Īśvara exists, but he is not something that arises. This is not the same as our internal [Buddhist] tenet.
This applies equally to the claim that things arise from primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) establish that there is an effect without a cause, asserting that the effect arises spontaneously.
Therefore, to refute the non-Buddhists, it is said that this thing exists because its cause exists; thus, the matter of the effect is established.
The reason for clarifying these two meanings is to demonstrate that birth occurs because causes and conditions are complete.
If the existence of this thing results from the existence of that thing, this is the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya).
If the arising of this thing results from the arising of that thing, this is the meaning of "cause" (hetu).
Regarding the "possessor of existence" (bhavāṅga): the place of birth is itself the cause and condition for birth.
This essence of the bhavāṅga-consciousness is a dharma of karmic retribution; it is definitively neutral by nature (avyākṛta).
Regarding the four types of existence (*bhava*): from the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to the age of six is "existence at birth" (*upapattibhava*);

from the age of seven onwards, until one is capable of discriminating between the ripening of karma and giving rise to craving, and until the relinquishing of life, is "existence as karma" (*karmabhava*);
"existence at death" (*maraṇabhava*) consists of a single moment, while "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Within the existence of becoming (*bhava*), the six consciousnesses give rise to three types of karma: wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable.

When the conditioned *bhavanga*-consciousness has ceased, the six consciousnesses that were sustained by it pass away; yet, through the sustaining power of the *bhavanga*-consciousness, they remain in operation.
Question: For what reason is the *bhavāṅga-vijñāna* (constituent-of-existence consciousness) established?

Throughout the duration of a single lifetime, it constantly takes a single object as its condition; if one is born among humans or devas, this consciousness perceives such karmic retributions as palatial towers and pavilions.
If the six consciousnesses arise, their coarse and obscuring functions prevent one from perceiving the activity of this consciousness.
If one is born into the evil realms, this consciousness takes only objects such as burning chariots as its conditions.
If the functioning of the six consciousnesses arising as retribution is powerful, one does not perceive the objects of these consciousnesses.
If the six consciousnesses of the desire realm take objects of desire as their conditions, ordinary beings cannot perceive this; the same applies up to the formless realm.

If the various consciousnesses of the formless realm cease, the function of this *bhavāṅga-vijñāna* becomes manifest, as is the case with the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for what is called a "seed," it is this continuous transformation that is capable of bringing about future retribution; this is termed a "seed."
Neither is the continuity itself without change nor is it the seed; nor is it the mere change without continuity that constitutes the seed.
Because continuity and change are inseparable, they together constitute the seed.
For example, the white color of a conch shell is neither identical to nor different from the conch.
If the white color were identical to the conch, then the conch would lack the three types of sensory objects;
if the white color were different from the conch, then one could perceive the white color without perceiving the conch.
It cannot be said that they are definitively different, because they are not different; thus it is called the "white conch.
The same applies to the transformation within the continuum, whereby it becomes the seed.
By the power of this perfuming, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is able to arise in the future.
The commentary states:
When the seeds, conditioned by the power of perfuming, are established, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) arises;
conditioned by future manifesting consciousnesses, the future differentiation of the six consciousnesses arises.
Therefore, regarding the fact that birth and death have no prior or subsequent parts:
if one is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma cannot arise.

If birth and death had a prior part, there would necessarily be a separate realm for sentient beings in that prior part where they would give rise to afflictions and karma to感召 (invoke) that prior part.
Since there is no prior portion of sentient beings initiating karma, there is no prior portion of birth and death; therefore, one knows that birth and death are without beginning and without origin.
These four points clarify their non-existence.

The first [state] is not the original source. If sentient beings were non-existent at the beginning and came into existence later, this non-existence could not serve as the basis for existence; there would be two kinds of fallacies:
first, if it is non-existent, it cannot produce what follows; if it can produce existence, then it is not non-existent. Second, there is the fallacy of parity:
if a flower in empty space could produce a material thing, then one might indeed derive existence from non-existence.
Second, because one does not perceive the birth of beings who have already abandoned desire, saṃsāra has no beginning.
If saṃsāra were initially free from greed and other afflictions, and only later possessed them, then even Arhats who have abandoned desire would necessarily give rise to desire again;
however, since such Arhats do not give rise to desire again, we know that saṃsāra has no beginning.
Third, because the practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) would be purposeless, saṃsāra has no beginning.

All noble ones (*ārya*) cultivate the eightfold noble path as a holy life in order to extinguish [defilements] so that they do not arise again; since those who have abandoned desire are no longer subject to birth and extinction, we know that saṃsāra has no beginning.
Fourth, there are two kinds of birth and death: first, retribution for evil; second, the paths of goodness.
This good and evil arises from the two causes of good and evil; it cannot be without cause.
Is this beginning of birth and death a path of goodness or a path of evil?
If it were a path of goodness, there would as yet be no cause for goodness;
if it were a path of evil, there would as yet be no cause for evil.
Because there is no third path apart from the two paths of good and evil, we know that there is no beginning.
An objection is raised:
"The beginning is spontaneous and does not depend on causes and conditions, whereas the end must depend on causes and conditions."
If that were so, this interpretation would be incorrect.
There are two faults:
first, it would contradict the principle of equality; second, cause and effect would not be analogous.

If you claim that birth and death are not caused by conditions at first, but later are caused by conditions, this is inconsistent; since both the beginning and the end are birth and death, why is one caused by conditions while the other is not?

Regarding the second point, "non-similarity": the effect also has a cause, and the cause also has a cause; because both cause and effect have causes, they attain similarity, and if they are similar, they can produce their own kind.
If for you there is no cause in the prior [moment], then there should likewise be no cause in the subsequent [moment].
If there were no cause in the prior [moment] but a cause existed in the subsequent [moment], then production would be impossible.
If it were possible to produce [something without a cause], then beans should produce wheat, and wheat should also produce beans.
Since this is not the case, we know that your claim that the preceding moment acts as the cause for the subsequent fruit means that the preceding cause is not actually a cause.

The Buddha spoke in verse; the first line reveals that consciousness is precisely the ālayavijñāna, and the ālayavijñāna is the retributive consciousness (vipākavijñāna), while the discriminating consciousness is the consciousness of afflictions (kleśavijñāna).
From the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the afflicted consciousness (*kleśavijñāna*) arises; this afflicted consciousness refers to the *ādānavijñāna* and so forth.

The second phrase clarifies that from affliction, consciousness arises, and from consciousness, perfuming (*vāsanā*) arises. This perfuming is precisely the functional capacity of karma, which is able to transform the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) into seed-consciousness (*bījavi-jñāna*).
The next phrase describes how retribution arises from karma.
The subsequent phrase summarizes the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
As for this "cycle," because it is not fixed, either causes may transform into effects, or effects may transform into causes.
Regarding the statement that "there are two kinds of perfuming," the following is intended to clarify two meanings:
first, to show that the means for cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is termed "false" and also "contrary"; second, to show that the means for nirvāṇa is termed "correct" and also "conformable."
Regarding those who cling to the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), all phenomena possess three natures:
first, the nature of conceptual construction; second, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to all phenomena as manifested through names and verbal expressions.
The nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*) refers to all phenomena as manifested through the principle of cause and effect.
The nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
The imagined nature has the absence of marks as its essence.
The dependent nature has the absence of arising as its essence.
Regarding the term "essence," there are five meanings:

First is the meaning of the category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): all things such as jars and garments do not depart from the category of the four great elements; being of the same nature as the four great elements is the meaning of intrinsic nature.

Second is the meaning of the nature of cause: the principle that all noble dharmas of the four foundations of mindfulness take this as their object; because one can generate noble dharmas by taking this principle as an object, it also carries the meaning of "cause."
Third is the meaning of "arising" (*jāti*). If things were without arising, their nature (*prakṛti*) would be invisible; since the meaning of arising is visible, nature is defined as arising.
The fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*) is the meaning of the nature of arising.
When the Tathāgata correctly teaches, sentient beings who believe and rejoice give rise to three kinds of faith:

first, faith that there is a true principle; second, faith that one can attain the merits of the fivefold Dharma-body; and third, faith that one will cultivate the fivefold body to fulfill the virtues of self-benefit and benefiting others.
Because the fivefold Dharma-body arises as the manifestation of the nature of attainment (*prāpti*), the meaning of the arising of the fivefold Dharma-body is that this constitutes its nature.

Regarding the fourth point, the meaning of "indestructible": this nature is unstained when in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and unpurified when in the state of a noble one (*ārya*); therefore, it is called "indestructible."
Regarding the meaning of the five secret treasuries (*pañca-guhya-kośa*): when one draws near to them, conduct becomes pure; when one opposes them, one remains far removed from them.
Because this Dharma is difficult to attain and profoundly hidden, it is called "secret" (*guhya*), which is precisely the meaning of "treasury" (*kośa*).
There are four kinds of birth:
first, birth through contact, such as when a man and woman unite and a child is conceived.
Second, birth through smelling, such as among species like cattle and sheep; when the male and female possess desire, the male smells the female’s organ and a child is immediately conceived.
Third, birth from sand: as with chickens, sparrows, and the like, when a female sparrow gives rise to a desire, she buries herself in dust and sand, and subsequently produces eggs and offspring.
Birth from sound occurs, as in the case of cranes, peacocks, and other such species; upon hearing the cry of the male with a mind of desire, they also lay eggs and give birth to offspring.
All those born from eggs are not to be eaten, for they all possess young.
The nature of conceptual construction is the emptiness of non-existence, because no phenomena can be apprehended through such construction.
The nature of dependence is the emptiness of being otherwise; in this way, that which is grasped is refuted.
The nature of reality (*tathatā*) is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*); being devoid of the two selves—the self of persons and the self of phenomena—it is empty of intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is like a flower in the sky; it is absolute non-existence.

The dependent nature differs from a flower in the sky; like a magical illusion, it is neither empty nor existent. Because one contemplates the dependent nature as being neither existent nor non-existent, one is able to attain the Path and become a Sage.
Emptiness and non-existence constitute nihilism; by contemplating emptiness and non-existence, one cannot attain the Way or become a sage.
All afflictions consist of distinct attachments to the nature of differentiation; all dharmas desire to contemplate and cultivate the nature of reality.
Attachment and the observation of habitual tendencies—these two belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
These two types of phenomena are called "perfumation" (*vāsanā*):
first, the perfumation of the seeds of afflictions; second, the perfumation of the seeds of the path.
Regarding the second [type of] perfuming that increases the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*):

because they are of the same kind, the fundamental consciousness gives rise to the four types of false attribution (*catur-viparyāsa*) by taking suchness (*tathatā*) as its object; this is the perfuming of delusion (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
Seeds and afflictions are both equally false; therefore, perfuming can cause the fundamental consciousness to increase.
For example, a sweet substance can cause that which is bland to increase; since the bland is also of a sweet nature, they being of the same nature, it can thus increase.
Regarding those who possess all capabilities, it is explained that there are four types of karma:

first, that which is performed but not prolonged. This refers to when a person of sharp intelligence encounters an evil friend and initiates unwholesome karma; because they immediately repent, that karma is not prolonged.

Second is being clothed but not acting: like a person of modesty who practices in accordance with others, this goodness is increased and expanded, yet because it cannot arise spontaneously from the mind, one does not act upon it.
Third, those that both perform and increase: for example, when a person performs wholesome karma and constantly practices it, this wholesome karma becomes increasingly vast.
Fourth, those that neither perform nor increase: these are untainted (anāsrava) wholesome karmas.
If that which further increases birth and death is designated as the "agent," then because the untainted (anāsrava) can eliminate birth and death, it is not an agent and thus does not increase.
The first three are karma; the latter one is partially not.
Among the first three [options], we take the third: that which both acts and is long. Therefore, it is said to be "endowed with all dharmas.
That which can produce the six destinies refers to the ability to obtain the retributive fruits of birth and death within the six destinies; it is the cause for the arising of the ālayavijñāna.

Because this body of birth and death is established through the skillful means of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), birth and death are brought to fulfillment; thus it is said that "this causal principle brings birth and death to fulfillment.
Second is the contemplation of the true nature of habituation: to contemplate the threefold absence of intrinsic nature is called contemplating the true nature of habituation.
Contemplation has four functions: first, contemplation for removal; second, contemplation for cessation; third, contemplation for realization; and fourth, contemplation for cultivation.
One contemplates the nature of the Truth of Suffering in this manner; the same applies to the other three truths.

Contemplating the suchness of the Four Noble Truths possesses four functions: contemplating suchness extinguishes suffering and extinguishes the origin; contemplating suchness is the realization of cessation; and harmonizing with suchness is the cultivation of the path.

Regarding "able to eliminate attachment to the nature of conceptualization": conceptualization constructs existence out of non-existence; because true contemplation reveals that existence contradicts intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is said to "eliminate" it.
The nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is that which is damaged by the first type of perfuming; it is damaged in the present and will be destroyed in the future.
If the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) is damaged, suffering (*duḥkha*) is also damaged.
When the *ālaya-vijñāna* is impaired, the sevenfold truth of suffering that was originally present is reduced to three layers, corresponding to the three realms.

Once these three layers have been impaired, although the *ālaya-vijñāna*—which is the basis for receiving karmic retribution—is no longer led by delusions and karma, it no longer enters birth within the three realms; rather, it undergoes birth within the four types of birth-and-death within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). In this manner, it eventually reaches the stage where there is no further birth-and-death.
Because the ālayavijñāna is impaired, rebirth is also impaired. Why is this?
Since manifesting consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is a discriminating consciousness, because manifesting consciousness is impaired, one knows that the discriminating consciousness is also impaired.
These consciousnesses that differentiate the self and the six sense objects have already been extinguished; how could they possibly be merely "impaired"?
What is here called "impairment" is spoken of in reference to the pure category (*śukla-pakṣa*).
This perishes together with the fundamental consciousness; it is the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which is capable of descending, that can be extinguished. — *Xiǎnshí lùn* (Treatise on Manifesting Consciousness)
